newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franco-German defence pact draws contrasting flak.
newsitem.headline: Franco-German defence pact draws contrasting flak.

text.p: A Franco-German defence pact has triggered contrasting reactions in Paris and Bonn, with controversy in France about the role of NATO and the United States and questions in Germany about its nuclear implications.

The joint strategy document, finally published on Wednesday after it was leaked to the newspaper Le Monde last week, says the two countries' security interests are inseparable, that their first commitment is to defend NATO and that they agree to discuss the role of nuclear deterrence in European defence.
While debate in consensus-loving Germany has largely been confined so far to newspaper commentaries, fierce criticism has come from the French parliamentary left.

France's conservative government fuelled suspicion by failing to distribute the text, agreed by President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Nuremberg on December 9, in parliament until after a German text was leaked to Le Monde.

After what government spokesman Alain Lamassoure played down as a "misunderstanding" but Gaullist defence expert Pierre Lellouche branded "this blunder", the government agreed to an emergency debate on the document on Wednesday afternoon.

The opposition Socialists and Communists have raised some fundamental objections to the Joint Franco-German Security and Defence Concept, charging that it subordinates European defence interests to the U.S.-led NATO alliance.
"This text shows a shift similar to the one Mr Chirac made on NATO by reintegrating France into NATO without obtaining any concession from the Americans," Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said.
Left-wing former defence minister Jean-Pierre Chevenement accused the government of selling out to Germany and NATO in a secret deal struck behind parliament's back.

The Communists accused the Gaullist-led government of having surrendered national defence sovereignty in a betrayal of General Charles de Gaulle, who pulled France out of NATO's U.S.-dominated military wing in 1966.
Although France has played a fuller role in the Atlantic Alliance under Chirac than it has at any time since De Gaulle, it has not yet fully returned to NATO's integrated command.
Paris is holding out for improbable U.S. concessions giving Europeans control of the alliance's southern command in Naples before announcing its decision at a summit in Madrid in July.
In Germany, the conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung called the document a useful wake-up call, but said it was little more than a list of good intentions.

"A joint strategic concept for the armed forces, as is often seen in cases like Rwanda, cannot be brought about by wishful thinking but only on the basis of concrete joint interests," the newspaper said in an editorial.

The liberal Sueddeutsche Zeitung pointed to the main German worry, questioning whether Bonn was being drawn into a back-door nuclear alliance with Paris which contradicted its post-war renunciation of nuclear weapons.
German government spokesmen were quick to deny any such risk in a joint briefing on Tuesday.

"A Franco-German nuclear entente would above all serve French interests," Sueddeutsche Zeitung commentator Kurt Kister warned. He said it could alienate Germany from the United States while allowing France to manoeuvre between Bonn and Washington.
In Paris, strategic analyst Dominique Moisi of the French Institute of International Relations said France was making more concessions than Germany.
"In some ways, France is moving more than Germany, by recognising it as a full partner in security," Moisi said.

"The old imbalance between a politically superior France and an economically superior Germany has been broken. France is recognising that Germany is economically superior and politically equal to it," he told Reuters.
But he said the French debate was artificial and no one would take to the streets to demonstrate against closer defence ties with Germany.
